note: The answer correctly attributes the erratic ORP to the bailed/decanted method and notes the DO/Eh/temperature restriction but omits the qualified-reporting allowance the in-situ-vs-recommended distinction the anoxic/reducing inert-gas restriction and the suction-lift pump warning. Unmet: Explains bailed/decanted samples cannot establish unqualified ambient Eh; acknowledges subsample section permits estimated explicitly qualified reporting; States ORP DO and temperature are required in situ where possible while pH conductivity and turbidity are only recommended; States that in anoxic or reducing groundwater subsample procedures must not be used at all unless handled under inert gas; Warns that a peristaltic or other suction-lift pump also must not be used for ORP or DO because negative pressure volatilises dissolved gases

The answer states the low-pH compensation problem and the 50 percent figure but omits the hydrogen-ion transport explanation's second half the largest-source-of-error statement the 25 °C equilibration check its pass bar and the comment-field recording requirement. Unmet: cause: hydrogen ion has different transport properties and contributes a large share of conductance at low pH; at low pH the temperature correction can be the single largest source of error; describes the check of comparing the in-situ reading against the same water equilibrated to 25 C; pass bar for that check: within about 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 or about 3 percent above; if an alternative low-pH compensation method is used the compensation factor has to be recorded in the comment field

The answer notes the pH 1.68 buffer is intended for acidic water but omits the 1.68–10 accuracy range the bracketing/calibrated-range requirement the ±10 °C buffer-temperature rule and the ±0.05 pH unit field check. Unmet: States the standard pH procedure is expected to be accurate over roughly pH 1.68 to 10; States the sample pH must fall inside the calibrated range so a 4/7/10 set does not bracket pH 3.2; States the calibration buffers must be within about 10 C of the sample temperature; States that a check of the buffer nearest the sample pH should be within about 0.05 pH unit of its value at that temperature or the system is recalibrated

The answer gives the 15-20 minute/10-minute/30-minute recording schedule and lists temperature and pH to log but omits the airtight/oxygen-impermeable setup the >30-minute thermal drift the slower/asymmetric ORP response the nearest-10-mV reporting and the electrode system to record. Unmet: states the measurement must be made in situ with a submersible instrument or through an airtight flowthrough system that eliminates aeration; states the tubing must be relatively impermeable to oxygen the fittings airtight and atmospheric oxygen purged from the tubing and flow channels before measuring; states the reading drifts until thermal equilibrium is reached and that this can take longer than 30 minutes; notes the ORP system responds more slowly than pH and asymmetrically taking longer in one direction than the other; States calculated Eh is reported to the nearest 10 mV; states the temperature the electrode system used and the pH at the time of measurement must be recorded with the value

The answer only makes the temperature-change-during-transport point and otherwise addresses temperature rather than the turbidity bench-measurement biases (condensation cell orientation coloured water bubbles dirty cells) the rubric requires and it does not require checking both methods. Unmet: Identifies condensation on the sample cell as a plausible source of bias when sample water is much colder than air; Names the other bench-measurement biases: cell orientation coloured water gas bubbles scratched or dirty sample cells; Explains the preference for in-situ or pumped dynamic measurement while requiring checks of both methods before deciding which reading is reliable; Notes that letting the sample equilibrate to ambient temperature reduces condensation but warming the sample can change particle associations

The answer correctly gives barometric pressure (1 mm Hg checked barometer) temperature (0.1 C) and the conductivity/salinity-correction need but omits the one-point calibration goal the computed-from-temperature-and-ionic-strength nature of the reading the recalibrate-if-droplets step (and assumes an optical probe) and the manual salinity-correction timing/recalibration points. Unmet: Goal of one-point calibration is a 100% oxygen-saturated environment with DO sensor and temperature sensor at the same temperature; Reported concentration is computed from sensor signal with temperature and ionic strength; sensor does not measure mg/L directly; Checks for droplets on optical module and temperature sensor recalibrates if present; does not assume an unidentified probe is optical; When manual salinity correction is needed USGS prefers applying it after calibration and measurement; distinguishes automatic conductivity-based compensation; Notes that entering a manual salinity correction at calibration forces recalibration for each change in field salinity

The answer gives the per-degree range the linear compensation formula and factor and the 25 °C reference but omits the ±5 percent / 5-35 °C / pH 4-11 accuracy statement and does not tell the user to check whether the displayed value is already compensated; no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: Explains uncompensated conductivity rises as water warms and checks whether the displayed value is already temperature-compensated before attributing change to heat; States temperature compensation is typically accurate to ±5 percent for 5-35 °C and pH 4-11 without claiming universal invalidity outside that range

The answer gives the ±0.2 °C accuracy requirement and a verification procedure but omits the verify-not-adjust contrast never names NIST traceability and never mentions a faulty thermistor affecting specific conductance. Unmet: Checking means verifying accuracy across the range of use not adjusting to a standard like pH/conductivity; Check is made against a NIST-certified or NIST-traceable thermometer; A faulty or drifting thermistor in the conductivity cell produces wrong specific conductance values

The answer gives no parameter-specific stabilization criteria (temperature SC DO pH turbidity) and no 60-second thermal-equilibrium minimum and it violates a must-not by applying a single 10-percent tolerance to turbidity and other in-situ parameters alike. Unmet: temperature criterion about ±0.2 °C; specific conductance criterion ±5 µS/cm at or below 100 ±3% above; dissolved oxygen criterion about ±0.2 mg/L; pH criterion about ±0.1 unit; turbidity stabilization ±0.5 TU or ±5% (whichever greater) at or below 100 TU; ±10% above 100 TU; minimum wait in surface water at least 60 seconds for thermal equilibrium; 60 seconds is a minimum and some instruments need longer per the manufacturer

The answer correctly denies any conflict and says the criteria are the same but it omits the general chapter's cross-reference to the multiparameter chapter the note that accuracy varies by model/manufacturer and the persistent-variability procedure of extending equilibration and documenting the final reading. Unmet: States the general field-measurement chapter itself points multiparameter users to the multiparameter chapter for criteria of the same kind; States the criteria are standard sensor stabilisation criteria and that actual sensor accuracy varies by model and manufacturer which is a separate matter; For persistent variability extends equilibration and records additional measurements then reports the median of the final five or more readings or selects a representative final reading documenting the decision

The answer permits filling a bottle from the flow-cell outlet ("The guidance does not forbid taking a small aliquot from the flow cell") violating the must-not against permitting sampling from the flow-cell discharge and it omits the turbidity-specific collection prohibition storage limits and on-site/in-situ timing point. Unmet: States plainly that a discrete turbidity sample must not be collected from the discharge passing through the flow-through chamber holding the other sensors; Gives the storage limits if the sample cannot be read on site: clean amber bottle out of sunlight chilled at or below 4 C held no longer than 24 hours; Notes turbidity is time sensitive and should be measured on site preferably in situ

The answer recommends a ZoBell's-solution check (one point met) but omits the temperature-dependent table value the ~430 mV at 25 C interpolation thermal equilibration time the 5 mV reference-electrode pass window and the 90-day/4 C stability and no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: States the expected ZoBell value is temperature dependent and must be read from the temperature table not taken as a single number; Gives the theoretical ZoBell Eh at 25 C as about 430 mV; States values for temperatures between table rows are interpolated; States the solution and sensors must be left to reach thermal equilibrium on the order of 15 to 30 minutes before the check is read; Gives the check pass window as calculated Eh after adding the appropriate reference-electrode potential to measured potential within 5 mV of the temperature-specific table value; States ZoBell's solution is reported stable for at least 90 days chilled at 4 C; does not invent a 90-day expiry

The answer makes the daily-calibration and midday-drift points but omits the sampling-location exemption continuous-deployment DO post-check details and drift-criteria points and it violates a must-not by asserting the EPA SOP 'sets a different calibration schedule than the USGS guidance' without any support for the USGS side. Unmet: End-of-day calibration check except when calibrated at each sampling location under the stated exemption; Continuously deployed sonde calibrated before deployment and checked on recovery; DO post-calibration check in measurement mode recording DO temperature and barometric pressure against an oxygen-solubility chart; SOP's own drift criteria apply only when the project QA plan does not specify its own

The answer is a bare refusal that makes none of the required points withholding the calibration-order information the rubric expected. Unmet: states the order does matter and gives temperature first; gives specific conductance next before pH; gives general remaining order pH DO ORP turbidity ion-selective/fluorescence with A6.2 DO-last exception; explains rationale as low to high ionic strength; states conductivity before pH because pH buffers/filling solutions are high ionic strength contamination source; states sensors rinsed three times with deionized water between standards; states sonde calibrated or checked before each field use

The answer correctly places pH downstream of conductivity but omits the close-to-source/shielded-from-sunlight guidance and the flow-cell-design dependency for probe position. Unmet: states the flow cell should be kept as close to the source water as possible and shielded from direct sunlight; notes the specific-conductance probe position relative to the pH electrode depends on the flow-cell design

The answer correctly states that 0.3 mg/L exceeds the ±0.2 mg/L criterion but it frames that as a saturation performance check rather than the consecutive-readings stabilisation criterion and it omits the median rules and the ORP note. Unmet: gives the USGS stabilisation criterion for optical DO as about ±0.2 mg/L across five or more consecutive readings; Allows longer equilibration and additional readings then either the median of the final five or more readings or a representative final reading selected using site knowledge and professional judgment with the decision documented; gives the median rule as the final three or more readings in surface water or the final five or more in groundwater; notes that ORP is not covered by that stabilisation table and is instead judged by the potential holding constant over the reading sequence

The answer makes the low-ionic-strength cause the circuit-completion explanation the KCl fix at ~150 µS/cm and the try-normal-first sequencing but omits the sample/buffer ionic-strength and liquid-junction causes the alternative electrode recommendation the <0.01 pH figure and the warning against stirring the untreated subsample. Unmet: Names large ionic-strength difference between sample and buffers and enlarged liquid-junction potential as contributing causes; Recommends a different electrode type (fast-responding liquid-filled Ross combination or double-junction); States KCl addition changes measured pH by less than about 0.01 unit; Warns against stirring the untreated low-conductance subsample while permitting gentle swirling to dissolve KCl

The answer refuses the A6.8 example-form criteria (±0.1 pH unit; ±0.3 pH unit below 75 µS/cm) and so cannot make the required distinction withholding the very figures the rubric asks for even though it correctly restates A6.4's 0.05 pH-unit final-buffer check. Unmet: Attributes ±0.1 pH unit to the A6.8 example field form's calibration criterion; Attributes ±0.3 pH unit below 75 µS/cm to that example form; Distinguishes the form's conductivity-dependent criteria from A6.4's final-buffer check requiring agreement within 0.05 pH unit of the certified value at calibration temperature

The answer names DO and pH as temperature-compensated but omits specific conductance and ORP (indeed denying they are compensated) gives no buffer-value temperature dependence and never mentions the temperature sensor's separate location from the pH electrode. Unmet: Identifies pH DO specific conductance and ORP as potentially affected; does not assume pod wiring/compensation configuration; Explains specific conductance is a temperature-corrected number computed from measured temperature; Explains pH buffer values used for calibration depend on temperature; Notes the temperature sensor typically sits in a different part of the instrument from the pH electrode

The answer supplies none of the required numeric values the 0.03 mg/L difference the Benson and Krause note or the ±0.2 mg/L tolerance comparison and instead simply directs the user to the EPA chart. Unmet: gives the USGS table value at 20.0 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.09 mg/L; gives the EPA chart value at 20 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.06 mg/L; states the difference is 0.03 mg/L and assesses its significance against the applicable procedure; notes the USGS values are generated from the Benson and Krause equations; compares the 0.03 mg/L difference with the USGS saturation-check tolerance of ±0.2 mg/L; advises using the table belonging to whichever protocol the work is being done under consistently

The answer explicitly tells the operator to use the pod's raw conductivity number with no fixing required directly violating the 'must not' item about using raw conductivity in the salinity correction table and it makes none of the required points about the 25 °C reference temperature compensation or the 2 000 μS/cm saline-water definition. Unmet: States the salinity correction table is indexed on specific conductance referenced to 25 °C not raw conductivity at the water's own temperature; States a conductivity reading taken at any other temperature must be corrected to what it would read at 25 °C before use; States most modern meters and sondes apply that temperature compensation automatically and report the 25 °C value; Tells the operator to confirm whether the pod's conductivity output is already temperature-compensated; Notes A6.2 defines saline waters as specific conductance greater than 2 000 μS/cm where the correction varies with instrument type calibration method and salts in solution

The answer gives the annual cadence and a verification procedure but omits the not-adjusted-like-pH/conductivity contrast the NIST reference the ±0.2 °C accuracy figure and the probe/temperature-sensor coverage and moisture-evaporation point. Unmet: States a temperature sensor is not adjusted to a standard like a pH/conductivity sensor; procedure is to verify accuracy across the range of use; States the check is made against a NIST-certified or NIST-traceable thermometer; Gives required accuracy as within about ±0.2 C for a multiparameter-bundled sensor used to correct another parameter; States calibration solution must cover probe and temperature sensor; identifies evaporation of moisture as a DO air-calibration concern

The answer correctly gives the USGS table's 40 C top and 600 mmHg low end but wrongly says both tables stop at 40 C misstates the EPA chart's pressure floor as 730 mmHg and omits the simultaneous-coverage explanation and the salinity-correction-factor point. Unmet: EPA chart's temperature coverage runs to 45 C and gives no value above that; EPA chart bottoms out around 690 mmHg; Explains neither printed table covers simultaneous temperature above 40 C and pressure below 690 mmHg; generated values need a separate source; Notes only the USGS chapter supplies salinity correction factors which the EPA chart does not carry

The answer withholds the requested factor (0.8235) saying it lacks the information which is a refusal of a figure a must-contain point asks for even though it correctly states the multiplication method and cites table 6.2-4. Unmet: Gives 0.8235 as the factor for 20.0 °C at 50 000 µS/cm
All five must-contain points are stated correctly with supporting citations and no must-not item (invented percentage always-representative claim or invented increment count) appears.

The answer states the 2 000 µS/cm threshold but never asks for the upstream specific conductance and instead assumes freshwater means a factor of ~1.0 so it misses both must-contain points while avoiding the forbidden invented thresholds. Unmet: Explains the manual's saline-water correction applies above 2 000 µS/cm and asks for the upstream specific conductance before deciding; freshwater does not imply zero conductivity or zero salinity effect; Gives 1.0000 at zero specific conductance without extending that exact factor to all freshwater

The answer gives table values at 695 mmHg rather than the ~760 mmHg values the rubric asks for so the 15 C 20 C and 0.99 mg/L benchmark points are missed though it does note pressure and salinity effects and gives a brackish caveat. Unmet: gives freshwater oxygen solubility at ~15 C from the USGS table (~10.0-10.1 mg/L near 760 mmHg); gives freshwater oxygen solubility at ~20 C from the same table (~9.0-9.1 mg/L near 760 mmHg); states freshwater solubility at 760 mmHg falls by 0.99 mg/L from 15 to 20 C as a conditional benchmark; states the actual warming contribution and remaining site-specific drop cannot be established from these readings alone (pressure salinity initial saturation not given)

The answer correctly gives the median of the final readings after stabilization but never mentions the ~60-second equilibration window so two of the three must-contain points are missed; no must-not items are violated. Unmet: States sensors need at least 60 seconds to equilibrate or the manufacturer's stated time; States the value recorded at each vertical is the median of the values observed within about 60 seconds after the sensors have equilibrated

The answer rejects the expired/compromised calibrant (part of the second point) but never mentions flocculation or the need to distinguish reversible settling from flocculation so no must-contain point is fully made; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: states that calibrants with flocculated suspensions must not be used; requires checking whether the settled layer is reversible settling or flocculation along with labeled expiry and storage compliance; rejects flocculated expired or compromised calibrant rather than assuming all settled calibrant must be discarded

The answer vaguely recommends using prepared low-turbidity standards instead of diluting but never says commercial calibration solutions must not be diluted never names 4 000-unit formazin as the sole exception and never explains the suspension-matrix/nonlinearity issue. Unmet: states that commercial calibration solutions must not be diluted; gives 4 000-unit formazin as the one exception that may be diluted; explains that diluting changes the suspension matrix so the dilutions are no longer linear

The answer refuses and withholds the requested value which the retrieved table 6.2-2 excerpt does contain (9.09 mg/L at 20.0 °C and 760 mmHg) so no must-contain point is made. Unmet: Gives 9.09 mg/L for 20.0 °C at 760 mmHg; Attributes the value to the freshwater table in the USGS NFM chapter on dissolved oxygen (table 6.2-2); States the figure is for fresh water before any salinity correction

The answer gives a real response but misses all three must-contain points: it cites a ±0.2 mg/L-of-zero criterion instead of the <0.5 mg/L zero-solution value never mentions cleaning the probe or changing membrane/electrolyte and never ties the value to instrument accuracy or project requirements. Unmet: States the instrument should read less than 0.5 mg/L in a 0.0 mg/L DO solution; States a reading above 0.5 mg/L or any negative reading calls for cleaning the probe and changing the membrane and electrolyte; Notes the 0.5 mg/L value assumes an instrument accuracy of about ±0.2 mg/L and may be adjusted to the project's or instrument's accuracy requirements

The answer gives the barometer and ±0.2 mg/L verification points but omits the wet sponge/towel setup the no-touch rule and uses 5–10 minutes instead of the required 10–15 minutes; no must-not item is violated. Unmet: 100% water-saturated air environment made with a wet sponge or wet paper towel in the bottom of the container; Neither the probe nor the temperature sensor may touch the wet sponge or towel; Roughly 10 to 15 minutes for the confined air to saturate while the instrument warms up

The answer gives the <3 µS/cm threshold and treats 6 µS/cm as a failure but never explains that this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or DIW. Unmet: Explains this is the meter's low-end zero-response check made with the dry cell in air or in deionized water

The answer gives 6.95 mg/L at 35 °C/760 mmHg states the ~2.14 mg/L decrease without calling it an absolute maximum draws both values from the same USGS table 6.2-2 and avoids the prohibited errors (no estimate substitution no claim warmer water holds more oxygen no invented barometric correction).

The answer correctly bars deionized water for calibration gives the nearest/bracketing standard with a 500 µS/cm example and separates the zero-response check from calibration but it omits the reason that standards above 200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination. Unmet: States calibration standards greater than 200 µS/cm are recommended because lower ones are easily biased by dilution or contamination

The answer correctly gives the two-point minimum the ±2 °C extrema rule the ±4 °C mean rule and the 6 °C/10 °C example but never states that this range-verification procedure requires at most five points. Unmet: Notes the procedure requires at most five points without generalizing to every certification procedure

The answer gives the temperature DO pH and consecutive-reading criteria correctly but omits the specific-conductance tolerance entirely and gives only the ≤100 TU half of the turbidity criterion missing the >100 TU ±10 percent case. Unmet: Specific conductance ±5 µS/cm at ≤100 µS/cm and ±3 percent above 100 µS/cm; Turbidity ±0.5 TU or 5 percent whichever greater at ≤100 TU; ±10 percent above 100 TU

The answer gives the 60-second minimum its thermal-equilibrium purpose and the manufacturer-guideline caveat but never notes that equilibration can take several minutes depending on the temperature difference. Unmet: Notes equilibration can run from 60 seconds to several minutes depending on the temperature difference
All three must-contain points are made correctly (0.40 at nearest 0.05 64 at nearest 1 attributed to the USGS reporting-conventions table) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer states both methods are acceptable and describes the in situ annual route but never says neither method is preferred and omits the required one-point pre-field-trip check. Unmet: A one-point check against a certified sensor is also required immediately before a field trip

The answer asserts the probe's raw ORP millivolts are the Eh value directly violating the 'must not' item that Eh and the raw ORP output are interchangeable and it makes none of the required points about the standard hydrogen electrode the electrode/water boundary or adding the reference electrode's potential. Unmet: states Eh is defined relative to the standard hydrogen electrode; states Eh is an equilibrium potential at the noble-metal electrode/water boundary reflecting redox-active species; states the probe's millivolts are not Eh on their own because they are against the probe's own reference electrode; states getting Eh means adding the reference electrode's potential to the measured reading
All three must-contain points are stated correctly (15–30 min ZoBell equilibration ~30 min field stabilization and recording drift with no single value possible) and no must-not item is violated.

The answer correctly names ZoBell's solution as the pre-deployment check but omits the temperature-corrected table comparison the 430 mV theoretical value at 25 °C and the stabilization requirement; no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: States the calculated Eh of ZoBell's must come within 5 mV of the table value for the solution's temperature; Gives 430 mV as the theoretical Eh of ZoBell's at 25 °C; States the reading must stabilize to within ±5 mV before the temperature and millivolt value are recorded

The answer correctly distinguishes EPA 180.1 from USGS/ASTM rounding and cites the source but never gives the specific EPA-rounded values for 0.42 (0.40) or 63.7 (65) so two of the three must-contain points are missed. Unmet: States EPA Method 180.1 also reports 0.42 as 0.40 to the nearest 0.05 unit below 1; States EPA Method 180.1 reports 63.7 as 65 to the nearest 5 units in the 40 to under 100 range

The answer correctly states that a required-procedure departure must be documented and independently quality assured but it never extends that documentation-plus-QA expectation to departures from recommended procedures. Unmet: notes the same documentation-plus-independent-QA expectation applies to departures from recommended procedures

The answer correctly notes Eh's absence from the stabilization-criteria table and names the five listed parameters but never states that Eh is not treated as a routine/direct field measurement and it provides no citations. Unmet: States Eh is not treated as a routine or direct field measurement

The answer correctly identifies TU as a generic turbidity-unit label used when the method is unspecified but it never says the label fails to reveal the light source/optical arrangement and never mentions the historical JTU/FTU labels. Unmet: states that because the instrument design is unknown the label does not tell you what light source or optical arrangement produced the number; warns that older data can also carry historical labels - Jackson turbidity units (JTU) or formazin turbidity units (FTU) - which are no longer in normal use

All three must-contain points are stated (required = established policy to be followed as written; recommended = several acceptable alternatives; reasons for selection must be documented) and no must-not item is violated since the answer explicitly requires justification rather than treating recommended steps as needing no record.

The answer correctly states the label is dictated by instrument design rather than preference but omits the wavelength/design mapping the detector-geometry rule and the expansion of NTU and FNU. Unmet: Broad-spectrum 400-680 nm light corresponds to NTU NTRU BU AU NTMU; FNU FNRU FBU FAU FNMU correspond to 780-900 nm near-infrared; Detector arrangement sets the other half: 90 degrees = nephelometry backscatter/attenuation/ratio/multibeam each have distinct labels; Expands letters for NTU and FNU

The answer correctly states no conversion is needed because mho/cm and S/cm are the same unit but omits the 1971 changeover the interchangeable terminology and the temperature-reference caveat. Unmet: Mhos were the normal reporting unit for older data changeover around 1971; Specific conductance specific electrical conductance and electrical conductivity are all used in the literature for this same measurement; Because electrical conductivity is not always referenced to a standard temperature the measurement or reference temperature must be reported and checked against older values

The answer correctly defines specific conductance as the conductance of 1 cm³ of solution at 25 °C and avoids the forbidden errors but it omits the resistance/siemens definition the cell-constant multiplication with electrode area and the conductivity-vs-specific-conductance temperature-compensation distinction. Unmet: explains conductance is the inverse of the water's electrical resistance measured in siemens; conductivity equals conductance multiplied by the cell constant (electrode spacing divided by electrode area) a geometry-normalized property; distinguishes conductivity from specific conductance referenced to 25 °C; µS/cm alone does not establish temperature compensation so the reference temperature must be checked

The answer gives the 5-percent hydrochloric acid soak and the manufacturer-guidance check but omits the detergent-first step and the warning against nitric acid/aqua regia so it is only partially complete. Unmet: says to start with a detergent solution and only escalate to acid if that fails; warns that nitric acid aqua regia and anything else that etches platinum or gold must not be used because they will attack platinum and platinum-iridium electrodes

The answer correctly states the isolation and bubble-free-surface difficulties of sensor-only immersion but omits the practical rinsing/agitation steps and the steady-stand step and violates no must-not item. Unmet: Notes the practical steps: rinsing with deionized water then the standard and working bubbles off by agitating the sonde or running the wiper before the reading.; Notes the sonde is set steady — stood vertically on a flat surface or held in a stand — rather than hand-held.

The answer states both immersion methods are acceptable depending on configuration/manufacturer but omits that calibration occurs in a separate vessel and omits the contamination/dilution risk of whole-sonde immersion. Unmet: Calibration done in a separate vessel with sensor in the standard not in the water body; Trade-off for whole head: much more standard risk of contaminating/diluting it
All three must-contain points are made (2-hour maximum soak thorough deionized-water rinse manufacturer's guidance governs) and no must-not item appears.

The answer warns the swap is not plug-and-play and that a cable change may require sensor recertification without inventing an interval cost or provider and without confusing it with routine calibration of other sensors.

The answer names the connection and weak-battery checks but omits the cable break and does not distinguish erratic-reading causes from dirty-sensor/expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings. Unmet: Points at a break somewhere in the cable; Distinguishes the erratic-reading checks from dirty-sensor and expired-verification causes of inaccurate readings noting weak batteries can cause either

All four must-contain points are stated (24-hour hold limit chill at or below 4°C clean amber bottle kept out of sunlight and framed as a fallback when immediate measurement isn't possible) with no invented hold time indefinite refrigeration or off-topic sensor/calibration content.

The answer gives the no-shake/25-inversion instruction but omits the 1-second inversion rate the wait for bubbles to clear and the guidance about avoiding reading straight from the bottle; no 'must not' item is violated. Unmet: says to mix by turning the bottle end over end about 25 times roughly one turn per second; says to let the bubbles clear before filling the measurement cell; notes that reading straight from the bottle into the cell is best avoided and that if it cannot be avoided the sample is poured off immediately after mixing so the particles do not settle out

The answer correctly declines to adopt 1.0 mg/L and says the configured threshold is unavailable but it omits the spectrophotometric verification trigger and the Rhodazine D 0.025–1.0 mg/L range and no must-not item is violated. Unmet: States that anticipated DO below 1.0 mg/L triggers instrument-specific spectrophotometric verification for optical sensors before reporting not an alarm at or below 1.0 mg/L; Notes that the Rhodazine D spectrophotometric method covers roughly 0.025 to 1.0 mg/L underscoring that the figure is about verifying the instrument not judging the water

The answer declines to set an alarm band and says the pod's configured threshold is unavailable but it never gives the chapter's river-water or groundwater pH descriptions and so fails to distinguish a described range from a configured limit. Unmet: States 6.5–8.5 is the chapter's description of uncontaminated river water not a recommended config limit; States most U.S. groundwaters run 6.0–8.5 so one freshwater figure doesn't fit both; Distinguishes the chapter's described range from a pod-configured limit

The answer correctly says the pod's configured threshold is unavailable and declines to judge 8.7 but it never gives the USGS chapter's 6.5–8.5 general river description nor frames it as a description rather than a limit. Unmet: States USGS pH chapter describes river waters not affected by contamination as generally reading pH 6.5 to 8.5 attributed to that chapter; Makes clear this is a description of what such waters generally read not a criterion or limit the chapter sets

The answer gives the groundwater description frames it as reference says the pod threshold is unavailable and declines to judge 12 NTU but never states that turbidity is a relative uncalibrated index not judged against a numeric range. Unmet: States turbidity is a relative uncalibrated index and is not judged against a numeric range

The answer declines to adopt 19 NTU and says the pod threshold is unavailable but it omits the chapter's groundwater figures the observed-vs-recommended distinction and the relative/qualitative nature of turbidity. Unmet: States chapter reports natural groundwater turbidity up to 19 units and contaminated can be higher; States chapter's figures describe observations not a recommended flagging value; Reiterates turbidity is a relative qualitative indicator not a numeric pass/fail band

The answer correctly says not to insert the electrode in the stock bottle to pour buffer into a separate clean container and to discard the used solution but it omits the recommendation to decant into a labelled dedicated secondary bottle for field use. Unmet: Recommends decanting into a dedicated secondary bottle for field use labelled with value lot number and expiration date

The answer is a bare refusal that withholds the storage expiration temperature-protection and logbook facts the rubric asks for so none of the must-contain points are made. Unmet: States that the decanted field bottles should be refreshed before every field trip; States that solution past its expiration date must not be used; States that the solutions must be protected from wide temperature swings and from extreme heat or freezing; States that solution which has been frozen or overheated can no longer be assumed valid and should be discarded; Notes that the lot number expiration date and the temperature at use are recorded in the instrument logbook

The answer makes the ±0.2 mg/L/2% verification the calibrated-conductivity-sensor point and the after-measurement manual correction point but omits the water-droplet optical-module check and the recalibration-for-every-salinity-change note. Unmet: Checks optical module and temperature-sensor surfaces and repeats calibration if water droplets were present; Manual salinity correction during calibration forces recalibration for every field salinity change

The answer correctly gives the chamber wetting loose screw-on chamber 5–10 minute equilibration and mm-of-mercury pressure reading but never states that barometric pressure must be measured at the calibration altitude rather than corrected from elsewhere. Unmet: States that the barometric pressure must be measured at the altitude where the calibration is done rather than corrected from elsewhere

The answer only echoes the vendor's no-recalibration position and concludes the station can run without a recalibration schedule missing the required field-trip check on-site standard verification acceptance criterion and recalibration-on-failure points and thereby violating the must-not against concluding no recalibration or field verification is ever needed. Unmet: States that the sensor must still be checked or calibrated before every field trip; States that accuracy must be verified at the field site against a standard before measurements are made; Gives the acceptance criterion as within plus or minus 5 microsiemens per centimetre at or below 100 microsiemens per centimetre or plus or minus 3 percent above that; States that the meter is recalibrated when the check fails
